title: Queries on a Permutation With Key
description: Brute force to optimized: directly simulating a permutation with find-and-move-to-front operations, and how a Fenwick tree would generalize this for larger constraints.

sections.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key

content.title: Queries on a Permutation With Key

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a permutation P of the m integers from 1 to m, and an array queries, process each query by finding the current index (0-based) of the value queries[i] inside P, recording that index, and then moving that value to the front of P. Return the array of recorded indices.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Repeated \"find index, then move to front\" operations","Simulate directly with an array, tracking position changes each time"],["Small constraints (m up to 1000)","A direct O(m) per query simulation is well within limits"]]}

blocks.text: Maintain a permutation as an ordered list. For each query value, find where it currently sits, note that position, then move it to the very front, shifting everything before it one step to the right.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Most-Recently-Used Deck of Cards
blocks.text: Picture a deck of cards numbered 1 to m in some order. Each query names a card. You find its current position in the deck, remember that, then pull it out and place it face-up on top of the deck.

blocks.caption: For each query, find the index, record it, then move the value to the front

blocks.text: Before reaching for any advanced structure, notice the constraints are small (m up to 1000), so directly simulating the permutation with an array supports both operations comfortably within time limits.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The value in P needs to be found by its VALUE, not its index, so a linear scan (or a position-tracking map) is required for each query.

Observation 2: After finding it, removing it from its current spot and inserting it at index 0 shifts every element before it one position to the right.

Observation 3: With m and queries.length both bounded by 1000, doing this shift directly with an array (or a JavaScript splice/unshift pair) costs at most O(m) per query, O(m times queries.length) total, which is fast enough.

Observation 4: A more advanced Fenwick-tree-based approach exists for much larger m, using a doubling index space to represent "insert at a position more to the left than anything seen so far" in O(log m) per operation, but it is not required here given the constraints.
This leads to directly maintaining the permutation as an array, searching for each query value's index, recording it, and moving it to the front.
Maintain P as an array. For each query, scan for the value's index, record it, then remove and reinsert it at the front.

items: Initialize P as [1, 2, ..., m].
For each query value q, linearly scan P to find its index.
Append that index to the answer list.
Remove q from its position and insert it at index 0.

codes.python:
def process_queries(queries, m):
    P = list(range(1, m + 1))
    result = []
    for q in queries:
        idx = P.index(q)              # linear search for the value
        result.append(idx)
        P.pop(idx)
        P.insert(0, q)                 # move to front
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain array directly models the permutation, with each query handled by search + remove + insert-at-front.
No auxiliary index structure is required since the constraints permit an O(m) scan per query.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times queries.length), each query costs O(m) for the scan plus O(m) for the shift.
Space: O(m) for the permutation array.

Limitation: this is already efficient enough given m, queries.length both at most 1000 (at most one million operations), so this direct simulation is the accepted, expected solution for this problem's constraints.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Given the constraints, direct array simulation is already the intended solution, so "optimizing" here means writing the simulation as tightly and clearly as possible rather than switching data structures.

For much larger m (say, up to 10^5 with many queries), a Fenwick tree over a virtual index space that starts at m and doubles leftward whenever a "move to front" needs a position further left than anything used so far, combined with a hashmap tracking each value's current virtual position, achieves O(log m) per operation.

Since this problem's constraints are small, the array-based simulation is presented as the primary, expected solution, with the Fenwick-tree idea noted as the technique that generalizes if constraints were larger (which is exactly why this problem is filed under the Fenwick Tree pattern group, even though direct simulation suffices here).

For these constraints, the array-based simulation IS the optimized, expected solution; the note above explains how the same idea would scale using a Fenwick tree if m and queries.length were much larger.

blocks.caption: A Fenwick tree over a large virtual index space supports fast position queries and front-insertions

items: Assign each of the m values a virtual position m, m+1, ..., 2m initially (using the back half of a doubled index space).
Mark each initial position as occupied in a Fenwick tree (a 1 at every occupied virtual index).

To find a value's current index among ACTIVE elements: use the Fenwick tree's prefix sum up to (but excluding) its virtual position, minus 1 (values that have been moved to the front and since removed no longer count).
To move a value to the front: assign it a new virtual position one less than the smallest virtual position used so far, mark it occupied, and unmark its old virtual position.

blocks.text: This mirrors the well-known "assign decreasing virtual timestamps for move-to-front operations, use a Fenwick tree for rank queries" technique, but for this problem's given constraints, the straightforward array simulation below is what is actually submitted.

codes.python:
def process_queries(queries, m):
    P = list(range(1, m + 1))
    result = []
    for q in queries:
        idx = P.index(q)
        result.append(idx)
        P.pop(idx)
        P.insert(0, q)
    return result

blocks.text: The permutation is small enough (at most 1000 elements) that maintaining it directly as an array, with a linear scan to locate each query value and a shift to move it to the front, correctly and efficiently reproduces the exact semantics described in the problem: find the current index, then reorder.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times queries.length) for the direct simulation, comfortably within limits for m, queries.length up to 1000.
Space: O(m) for the permutation array.

blocks.text: Queries on a Permutation With Key is a reminder that recognizing when constraints already permit a direct simulation is itself part of the pattern-matching skill, even inside a Fenwick Tree problem set.

items: Forgetting that indices are 0-based when recording the found position.
Moving the value to the front AFTER recording the index, not before (order matters).

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "given m up to 1000, an O(m) per-query simulation is acceptable, but here is how a Fenwick tree would generalize this for larger inputs" shows both practical judgement and depth.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "what if m were 10^5 instead of 10^3", think: assign decreasing virtual positions for move-to-front, and use a Fenwick tree for rank/prefix-sum queries.

items: How would you support this efficiently if m were up to 10^5 with 10^5 queries?
How would you support arbitrary move-to-position (not just move-to-front) efficiently?
LFU/LRU cache style "move to front on access" logic.
Any problem needing fast rank-of-value queries under insertions/deletions, solved with a Fenwick tree over a virtual coordinate space.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The direct array simulation runs in O(m times queries.length) time and O(m) space, which is optimal given the constraints of this specific problem.

items: Pattern: maintain a permutation directly as an array; for each query, find-index-then-move-to-front.
Core Idea: a linear scan plus array shift correctly and efficiently reproduces the required behavior given the small constraints.
Time: O(m times queries.length).
Space: O(m).
Most Important Observation: recognizing that constraints already permit direct simulation is itself a valid, expected answer.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once the "search + move to front" operation is understood; the Fenwick-tree generalization adds depth.
One line memory trick: find its spot, note it, then send it to the front.
